content: HIV prevalence can be calculated by determining the proportion of individuals who test positive for HIV among those with known HIV status (either tested negative or previously known to be HIV-positive). This proportion is then multiplied by 100% to express HIV prevalence as a percentage. Statistical models can be used to test for differences in site-level HIV prevalence between these rounds. To analyze trends in HIV prevalence over time, surveillance programs can examine site-specific or median prevalence trends at national or subnational levels, provided the surveillance methods have remained unchanged. Plotting prevalence data over time for specific demographic groups, such as age groups, can help identify changes in HIV infection levels. Graphical representations, such as scatter plots or line graphs, are particularly effective for visualizing trends, with prevalence estimates (and confidence intervals) on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. Ideally, at least four rounds of data should be used for graphical trend analysis. Statistical modeling can also be employed to estimate and test trends in HIV prevalence. In sentinel surveillance, the prevalence estimate is representative only of the population accessing the specific antenatal care (ANC) site where the data was collected. Aggregating data to calculate regional or national prevalence estimates is inappropriate because sentinel ANC sites are not representative of all ANC sites. Instead, the median of site-level prevalence estimates should be used as a summary statistic, as it minimizes the influence of outliers. The range of site-specific prevalence should also be reported to highlight differences between sites. However, the median is only a summary of site-level results and does not represent national or regional HIV prevalence among ANC attendees. For general population estimates, UNAIDS’ Spectrum analysis tools should be used. Routine data collection for HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC may include records with missing data. Surveillance programs should establish a consistent approach to handling such records, particularly for core surveillance variables. Missing data should be accounted for in the interpretation and dissemination of surveillance results, as they can impose limitations on the findings. Underperforming surveillance sites, such as those with incomplete data collection or substandard HIV testing quality, should be identified and targeted for support to improve program services and data quality. If a significant proportion of sites are underperforming, a retrospective approach may not be suitable, and real-time data collection through sentinel surveillance may be considered until routine systems are strengthened. HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC provides estimates of HIV prevalence among this population. However, several factors limit the generalizability of these results to other populations. For example, surveillance results may not represent all pregnant women attending ANC, particularly if sentinel sites are not probabilistically selected. Additionally, private ANC attendees, rural populations, and women who do not attend ANC may be underrepresented, introducing potential biases. HIV prevalence among ANC attendees may not accurately reflect prevalence among all women or the general population. Factors such as age of sexual debut, fertility patterns, and family planning practices can complicate the generalization of surveillance results. For instance, HIV prevalence among young pregnant women may not represent similarly aged women in the general population, as the latter includes women who have not had sexual intercourse. Similarly, HIV-associated fertility reductions and the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) can influence the representation of HIV-positive women among ANC attendees. HIV prevalence trends among ANC attendees may also differ from those in the general population due to differences in condom use, hormonal contraceptive use, and fertility intentions. For example, frequent condom use in the general population may result in higher HIV prevalence among ANC attendees compared to similarly aged women. Conversely, increased access to integrated HIV treatment and family planning services may reduce unintended pregnancies among HIV-positive women, potentially lowering HIV prevalence among ANC attendees relative to the general population. Finally, HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC excludes men and women beyond reproductive age, limiting its applicability to the general population. In generalized epidemics, where HIV prevalence is often higher among women, surveillance among ANC attendees may overestimate prevalence in the general population. Conversely, in concentrated epidemics with a higher burden among men or key populations, surveillance among ANC attendees may underestimate general population prevalence.
